places.summary: A village east of Paris, here called 'Montreuil-sur-le-Bois', near the forest of Vincennes. It is now Montreuil, a large town in Seine-Saint-Denis.
places.summary_fr: Un village à l'est de Paris, appelé ici « Montreuil-sur-le-Bois », près de la forêt de Vincennes. C'est aujourd'hui Montreuil, une grande ville de Seine-Saint-Denis.
places.summary_sv: En by öster om Paris, här kallad ”Montreuil-sur-le-Bois”, nära skogen i Vincennes. I dag är det Montreuil, en stor stad i departementet Seine-Saint-Denis.
places.detail:
The name Montreuil derives from the Latin Monasteriolum, meaning small monastery. By 1070, the lordship was held by Morard de Montreuil, a vassal of the king. The village grew in importance alongside the royal presence at nearby Vincennes, centred around the church of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul, where King Charles V and his wife Jeanne de Bourbon were baptised.

From 1260, Montreuil supplied water to the castle of Vincennes. In 1360, after suffering in the wars under King John the Good, the villagers were granted exemptions from taxes and forced labour on the condition that they maintained at their own expense the fountains that fed the castle fishpond. These privileges were confirmed in 1363 and 1380.

places.summary: A village on the Seine east of Paris, with riverside estates and, later, wine warehouses. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 12th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la Seine à l'est de Paris, avec des domaines au bord de l'eau et, plus tard, des entrepôts de vin. Il fut annexé à Paris en 1860 et fait aujourd'hui partie du XIIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En by vid Seine öster om Paris, med gods vid floden och, senare, vinlager. Den införlivades med Paris 1860 och är i dag en del av 12:e arrondissementet.
places.detail:
The name Bercy appeared in the twelfth century, derived from an Old French word meaning sheepfold. At the end of the fifteenth century, the domain was purchased by Antoine Robert, a royal secretary, before passing to the Malon family.

On the 1550 map and other contemporary views, Bercy is shown as a feudal fortress with a donjon, enclosed by stone walls and a fortified gate near the Seine. Downstream stood the manor of La Grange aux Merciers, a lavish residence with three main buildings capable of lodging forty horsemen, along with a windmill and outbuildings. Charles de Malon united the two seigneuries in 1624, later demolishing the fortified manor in 1658 to construct a new chateau.

places.summary: A village at the confluence of the Seine and the Marne, with a country house of the archbishops of Paris. It is now part of Charenton-le-Pont.
places.summary_fr: Un village au confluent de la Seine et de la Marne, avec une maison de campagne des archevêques de Paris. Il fait aujourd'hui partie de Charenton-le-Pont.
places.summary_sv: En by vid sammanflödet av Seine och Marne, med ett lantställe som tillhörde ärkebiskoparna av Paris. I dag är den en del av Charenton-le-Pont.
places.detail: In the Middle Ages, the parish of Conflans belonged to the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs following a donation in 1098. On the 1550 map, the village dominates the confluence of the Seine and Marne, alongside the church of Saint-Pierre and the remains of the 14th-century Séjour de Bourgogne. Nearby stood the feudal fortress of Bercy, the manor of La Grange aux Merciers, and the bridge of Charenton topped with towers. The bridge was a crucial crossing: seized by Vikings in 865, taken by the dauphin Charles in 1358, and retaken from the English on 11 January 1436. Downstream stood the Séjour du Roi, a fort built by Philippe le Bel attested in 1314 with stables for 50 horses; Louis XI gave it to Gillette Hennequin in 1481 before its dismantling in the early 17th century.

places.summary: A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Ivry-sur-Seine.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la Seine au sud-est de Paris, aujourd'hui Ivry-sur-Seine.
places.summary_sv: En by vid Seine sydöst om Paris, i dag Ivry-sur-Seine.
places.detail: The name derives from the Gaulish Eburiacum, meaning "place of yews", recorded as Ivriacum in a 936 charter of King Louis IV of France. In 52 BC, the territory saw battle between the Parisii leader Camulogenes and Caesar's lieutenant Labienus. By the 9th century, the land was held by the chapter of Notre-Dame. Construction of the parish church of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul began in the 12th century, with a square bell tower from the 13th century and a pillar bearing the date 1575. On the 1550 map, the village is shown under the spelling Iveri with its church. From the 13th century, the land was split between several religious bodies, including the abbeys of Saint-Magloire and Saint-Victor and the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, until a single lay lord bought the entire estate in 1659.

places.summary: A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Vitry-sur-Seine.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la Seine au sud-est de Paris, aujourd'hui Vitry-sur-Seine.
places.summary_sv: En by vid Seine sydöst om Paris, i dag Vitry-sur-Seine.
places.detail: The village derives its name from Victoriacum, meaning the domain of Victorius, and appears on the 1550 map spelled Viteri. In 52 BC, the plain of Vitry was the likely site of the Battle of Lutetia, where Roman forces under Titus Labienus defeated the Gaulish coalition led by Camulogenes. Vikings raided and burned the settlement in 886 and 887, destroying its church. In 1280, former serfs of the chapter of Notre-Dame established a farm and a river port known as Port-à-l'Anglais. During the Jacquerie in 1358 and the conflict between the dauphin Charles and Étienne Marcel, Port-à-l'Anglais witnessed heavy fighting, leading Charles to grant the inhabitants tax exemptions in 1370. Further conflict between Armagnacs and Burgundians brought pillage in 1434. By 1462, a parish survey recorded 47 households, or about 211 inhabitants.

places.summary: A village on the road south from Paris, now Villejuif.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la route partant de Paris vers le sud, aujourd'hui Villejuif.
places.summary_sv: En by vid vägen söderut från Paris, i dag Villejuif.
places.detail: The name Villejuif first appears in a papal bull issued by Pope Calixtus II on 27 November 1119 as Villa Judea, meaning "Jewish village". The spelling Villejuifve was used in later centuries. A 17th-century writer, Louis Moréri, claimed that the town was founded by Jews expelled from Paris, though no medieval records confirm this. In the 13th century, scribes from Notre-Dame occasionally recorded the name as Villa Jullitoe, likely confusing it with Saint Julitte, to whom the parish church is dedicated. Modern scholars have also suggested a derivation from a Gallo-Roman villa owner named Juvius, or from a 10th-century settlement called Gesedis, though the origin remains debated.

places.summary: A village on the Bièvre south of Paris, now Gentilly. Part of its territory was annexed to Paris in 1860.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la Bièvre au sud de Paris, aujourd'hui Gentilly. Une partie de son territoire fut annexée à Paris en 1860.
places.summary_sv: En by vid Bièvre söder om Paris, i dag Gentilly. En del av dess område införlivades med Paris 1860.
places.detail: The name Gentiliaco is recorded in the 7th century in Saint Ouen's biography of Saint Éloi, referring to foreign goldsmiths established here under the Merovingians. King Pepin the Short spent the winter of 762 and Easter of 766 in Gentilly, holding a council of bishops in 767. In 878, King Louis the Stammerer granted the lordship to Ingelwin, Bishop of Paris. During the late Middle Ages, the village possessed a motte castle, a fortified square tower, a mill, a bakehouse, a press, and stone quarries. King Louis IX founded a Carthusian monastery here in the 13th century. The parish church dates from the 13th and 15th centuries. During the Wars of Religion under Charles IX, the Prince of Condé encamped at Gentilly with his troops.

places.summary: The ruined castle of Bicêtre, south of Paris. Louis XIII had a hospital for invalid soldiers built on the site; it later became the Hôpital Bicêtre, in Le Kremlin-Bicêtre.
places.summary_fr: Le château en ruine de Bicêtre, au sud de Paris. Louis XIII fit construire sur le site un hôpital pour les soldats invalides ; il devint plus tard l'hôpital Bicêtre, au Kremlin-Bicêtre.
places.summary_sv: Den förfallna borgen Bicêtre, söder om Paris. Ludvig XIII lät bygga ett sjukhus för invalidiserade soldater på platsen; det blev senare Hôpital Bicêtre, i Le Kremlin-Bicêtre.

places.summary: A village on a hill north-east of Paris, whose springs supplied the city's fountains. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 (19th and 20th arrondissements).
places.summary_fr: Un village sur une colline au nord-est de Paris, dont les sources alimentaient les fontaines de la ville. Il fut annexé à Paris en 1860 (XIXe et XXe arrondissements).
places.summary_sv: En by på en kulle nordost om Paris, vars källor försörjde stadens fontäner. Den införlivades med Paris 1860 (19:e och 20:e arrondissementen).
places.detail:
The oldest settlement here was Savies, an estate granted in 862 by Charles the Bald to the abbey of Saint-Denis. In 1060, King Henry I gave Saint-Martin-des-Champs a large domain that included the farm of Savies. Nearby, the hamlet of Poitronville emerged in the twelfth century; its name was replaced by Belleville from the fifteenth century, first appearing in records in 1451.

Devastated during the Hundred Years' War in 1436, the village grew under Francis I along the road to Romainville. In 1543, a chapel dedicated to Saint John the Baptist and Saint Blaise was built to save residents the long journey to Saint-Merry in Paris.

places.summary: A village east of Paris, now Bagnolet.
places.summary_fr: Un village à l'est de Paris, aujourd'hui Bagnolet.
places.summary_sv: En by öster om Paris, i dag Bagnolet.
places.detail: The name derives from the late Latin balneoletum, recalling an ancient bathhouse. The parish church, dedicated to Saint Gilles and Saint Leu, was built around 1320 and appears on the 1550 map. By the 15th century, Bagnolet had become a residential retreat for high officials. After the execution of Jean des Mares in 1383, King Charles VI granted his house at Bruyères-lès-Paris—shown as Les Brières on the map—to his chamberlain Guillaume de La Trémoille. In 1412, Queen Isabeau of Bavaria acquired a château here equipped with gardens, a windmill, a winepress, and a dovecote. The estate passed to Tanneguy III du Chastel and later to Prégent de Coëtivy. Charles VI also granted the nearby manor of Mallassis to his mistress Odette de Champdivers, while John of Lancaster, English regent of France, acquired the Bois de Bagnolet in 1422.

places.summary: A village east of Paris, on the site of a Merovingian royal residence. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Antoine and is now a quarter of the 12th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un village à l'est de Paris, sur le site d'une résidence royale mérovingienne. Il fut absorbé par le faubourg Saint-Antoine et c'est aujourd'hui un quartier du XIIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En by öster om Paris, på platsen för en merovingisk kungsgård. Den uppgick i faubourg Saint-Antoine och är i dag ett kvarter i 12:e arrondissementet.

places.note: the hamlet of Popincourt outside the wall; its name survives in the rue Popincourt
places.summary: A hamlet north-east of the city, outside the wall. Its name survives in the rue Popincourt and the Popincourt quarter of the 11th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un hameau au nord-est de la ville, hors de l'enceinte. Son nom survit dans la rue Popincourt et le quartier Popincourt du XIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En liten by nordost om staden, utanför muren. Namnet lever kvar i rue Popincourt och kvarteret Popincourt i 11:e arrondissementet.
places.detail: The hamlet originated around 1400, when Jean de Popincourt, president of the Parlement of Paris under Charles VI, built a manor house at the junction of the Chemin Vert and a north-south lane connecting the abbey of Saint-Antoine-des-Champs to the faubourg du Temple. By 1550, a cluster of about fifteen houses had formed the hamlet outside the wall of Charles V. The Comte de Cheverny acquired the neighbouring estate of La Rochette, extending the manor's park, and built a country house called the Bel Esbat. In 1561, a Reformed Protestant place of worship opened on the property of Bertrand de Popincourt, but it was destroyed the following year by troops commanded by the constable Anne de Montmorency.

places.summary: A hamlet on the road to Belleville, known for its taverns: just outside the city, wine escaped the city's toll. It is now the area around the rue du Faubourg-du-Temple and Belleville.
places.summary_fr: Un hameau sur la route de Belleville, connu pour ses guinguettes : juste hors de la ville, le vin échappait à l'octroi. C'est aujourd'hui le secteur de la rue du Faubourg-du-Temple et de Belleville.
places.summary_sv: En liten by vid vägen till Belleville, känd för sina krogar: strax utanför staden slapp vinet stadens tull. I dag är det området kring rue du Faubourg-du-Temple och Belleville.
places.detail: The area began as an agricultural estate granted by King Henry I to the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in 1060. During the 13th century, wealthy Parisians built country houses with kitchen gardens, known as courtils, along the road leading to Romainville. The construction of the wall of Charles V turned the hamlet into an official suburb, the faubourg du Temple. During the Hundred Years' War, local estates were broken up and converted into vineyards producing a cheap light wine known as guinguet. Tavern keepers opened drinking houses, or guinguettes, to serve this tax-exempt wine outside the city limits, establishing La Courtille as a famous suburban entertainment district.

places.note: the marais: market gardens on the old marshland north of the wall (today the 10th arrondissement), not the Marais district
places.summary: The marais, market gardens on the old marshland north of the city wall, where vegetables for Paris were grown. Today the area is part of the 10th arrondissement; the Marais district inside the walls has the same origin.
places.summary_fr: Les marais, jardins maraîchers sur les anciens terrains marécageux au nord de l'enceinte, où l'on cultivait les légumes pour Paris. Le secteur fait aujourd'hui partie du Xe arrondissement ; le quartier du Marais, à l'intérieur des murs, a la même origine.
places.summary_sv: Le marais, handelsträdgårdar på den gamla sankmarken norr om stadsmuren, där grönsaker odlades för Paris. I dag ingår området i 10:e arrondissementet; stadsdelen Marais innanför murarna har samma ursprung.

places.summary: The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Martin, around the church of Saint-Laurent and the Saint-Laurent fair.
places.summary_fr: Le faubourg le long de la route partant de la porte Saint-Martin vers le nord, autour de l'église Saint-Laurent et de la foire Saint-Laurent.
places.summary_sv: Förstaden längs vägen norrut från Porte Saint-Martin, kring kyrkan Saint-Laurent och Saint-Laurentmarknaden.

places.summary: The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Denis towards the abbey of Saint-Denis. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis follows its main street.
places.summary_fr: Le faubourg le long de la route partant de la porte Saint-Denis vers le nord, en direction de l'abbaye de Saint-Denis. La rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis suit sa rue principale.
places.summary_sv: Förstaden längs vägen norrut från Porte Saint-Denis mot klostret Saint-Denis. Rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis följer dess huvudgata.
places.detail: The thoroughfare forms part of an ancient Roman road running from Lutetia to Beauvais. In the twelfth century, following the establishment of the Saint-Lazare fair by Louis VI, it became known as the chaussée Saint-Lazare. It served as a major route heading north towards Saint-Denis and its basilica, where the kings of France were buried. By 1636, a manuscript records it under the names Grand rue du faulxbourg Saint Denis and rue du faulxbourg Saint Lazare. The section running alongside the maison Saint-Lazare kept the name rue du Faubourg-Saint-Lazare until the First Empire, and during the Revolution in 1793 it was briefly renamed rue du Faubourg-Franciade.

places.summary: A suburb north of the city walls, the Villeneuve-sur-Gravois, where the church of Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle was built in the 16th century. It was destroyed during the siege of 1591 and later rebuilt; it is the Bonne-Nouvelle quarter of today.
places.summary_fr: Un faubourg au nord de l'enceinte, la Villeneuve-sur-Gravois, où l'église Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle fut construite au XVIe siècle. Détruit pendant le siège de 1591, puis reconstruit, c'est l'actuel quartier de Bonne-Nouvelle.
places.summary_sv: En förstad norr om stadsmurarna, Villeneuve-sur-Gravois, där kyrkan Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle byggdes på 1500-talet. Den förstördes under belägringen 1591 och byggdes senare upp igen; i dag är det kvarteret Bonne-Nouvelle.
places.detail: During the Wars of Religion in November 1562, all buildings in the settlement were razed when a Protestant army led by Condé and Coligny threatened Paris. The rampart of the Fossés Jaunes was created in front of the mound in 1566. During the siege of Paris by Henri IV in 1591, the Catholic League leveled the mills, houses, and the church that had been erected on the hill in 1563. Anne of Austria laid the foundation stone of a new church on the site in 1624. Around 1634–1635, the rampart was strengthened with a large bastion on its northern face, which was later demolished between 1680 and 1685 when the ditches were filled to create the Nouveau-Cours.

places.summary: A hamlet on the north side of the hill of Montmartre, now the Clignancourt quarter of the 18th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un hameau sur le versant nord de la butte Montmartre, aujourd'hui le quartier de Clignancourt dans le XVIIIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En liten by på Montmartrekullens norra sida, i dag kvarteret Clignancourt i 18:e arrondissementet.
places.detail:
The hamlet's name comes from Clenini Curtis, named after a Gallo-Roman villa owner. Documented from the thirteenth century on the northern slope of Montmartre, Clignancourt produced grain, cherries, and wine. The fief belonged to the abbey of Saint-Denis in the fourteenth century before passing to wealthy Parisian families.

During the siege of Paris in 1465, troops under Charles, Count of Charolais, ravaged the area. On 9 September, Breton and Burgundian soldiers stripped the vineyards of Clignancourt, harvesting unripe grapes to make wine. In 1569, the lordship was sold to Jacques Ligier, treasurer general of the Cardinal de Bourbon, who built a chapel dedicated to the Holy Trinity.

places.summary: The hill north of Paris with its village and the Benedictine abbey of Montmartre. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now the 18th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: La colline au nord de Paris, avec son village et l'abbaye bénédictine de Montmartre. Elle fut annexée à Paris en 1860 et forme aujourd'hui le XVIIIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: Kullen norr om Paris med sin by och benediktinklostret i Montmartre. Den införlivades med Paris 1860 och är i dag 18:e arrondissementet.
places.detail: The church of Saint-Pierre was founded in the sixth century and recorded in 850, though the village was pillaged by the Normans during the siege of 885. In 1133–1134, King Louis VI established the royal abbey of the Dames de Montmartre at the top of the hill. During the siege of 1590, Henri IV installed artillery batteries on Montmartre to bombard the streets of Saint-Honoré, Saint-Denis, and Saint-Martin. In 1686, the nuns abandoned the upper convent to settle at the abbaye d'en bas halfway down the slope. The seigneurial domain of the abbey extended over much of the surrounding area until the nuns were expelled in 1790 and the property was sold in 1794.

places.summary: A fortified farm north-west of the city, belonging to the bishops of Paris and later the Hôtel-Dieu, on a stream of the same name. The rue de la Grange-Batelière (9th arrondissement) keeps its name.
places.summary_fr: Une ferme fortifiée au nord-ouest de la ville, appartenant aux évêques de Paris puis à l'Hôtel-Dieu, sur un ruisseau du même nom. La rue de la Grange-Batelière (IXe arrondissement) en garde le nom.
places.summary_sv: En befäst gård nordväst om staden, som tillhörde Paris biskopar och senare Hôtel-Dieu, vid en bäck med samma namn. Rue de la Grange-Batelière (9:e arrondissementet) bär fortfarande dess namn.
places.detail: The fief covered 58 hectares of marshland that King Louis VII granted to the canons of Sainte-Opportune in 1153. It took its name in 1410, recorded variously as Granchia Batilliaca or Grange Bataillée, possibly named from the ferry used by local inhabitants to cross the Ménilmontant stream. The land belonged to the bishopric of Paris and the Laval family, owned in the early fifteenth century by Anne de Laval and Guy Turpin, before being acquired by Jean de Malestroit, bishop of Saint-Brieuc. From 1514 it passed to Jean Vivien and his heirs. Subdivisions began in 1575 for townhouses, and the principal farm building was converted into a private mansion in the eighteenth century before being demolished in 1847.

places.summary: The suburb that grew up around the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés outside Philip Augustus's wall, with the Saint-Germain fair. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became the most aristocratic quarter of Paris.
places.summary_fr: Le faubourg qui se développa autour de l'abbaye de Saint-Germain-des-Prés hors de l'enceinte de Philippe Auguste, avec la foire Saint-Germain. Aux XVIIe et XVIIIe siècles, il devint le quartier le plus aristocratique de Paris.
places.summary_sv: Förstaden som växte fram kring klostret Saint-Germain-des-Prés utanför Filip Augustus mur, med Saint-Germainmarknaden. På 1600- och 1700-talen blev den Paris mest aristokratiska kvarter.

places.summary: A hamlet north-west of the city with a manor house, later known for its open-air taverns. It is now part of the 9th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un hameau au nord-ouest de la ville avec un manoir, connu plus tard pour ses guinguettes. Il fait aujourd'hui partie du IXe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En liten by nordväst om staden med en herrgård, senare känd för sina utvärdshus. I dag är den en del av 9:e arrondissementet.
places.detail: The hamlet took its name from the Pocheron or Porcheron family, who owned houses here from 1290. In 1380, the Le Coq family bought the estate and altered the manor house, which became known as the château du Coq. It was owned by Hugues Le Coq, provost of the merchants of Paris from 1420 to 1429 and from 1434 to 1436, and remained in his family until the 18th century. King Louis XI stayed at the château on 29 August 1461 before entering Paris, following his coronation at Reims on 15 August. After the Revolution, the castle fell into ruin and was completely demolished in 1854 during Haussmann's works.

places.summary: The suburb along the road west from the Porte Saint-Honoré. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré follows its main street; the Élysée palace stands on it.
places.summary_fr: Le faubourg le long de la route partant de la porte Saint-Honoré vers l'ouest. La rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré suit sa rue principale ; le palais de l'Élysée s'y trouve.
places.summary_sv: Förstaden längs vägen västerut från Porte Saint-Honoré. Rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré följer dess huvudgata; Élyséepalatset ligger vid den.

places.summary: A village west of the city belonging to the bishop of Paris, hence its name (the bishop's town). The rue de la Ville-l'Évêque, near the Madeleine, keeps its name.
places.summary_fr: Un village à l'ouest de la ville appartenant à l'évêque de Paris, d'où son nom. La rue de la Ville-l'Évêque, près de la Madeleine, en garde le nom.
places.summary_sv: En by väster om staden som tillhörde biskopen av Paris, därav namnet (biskopens stad). Rue de la Ville-l'Évêque, nära Madeleine, bär fortfarande dess namn.

places.summary: A village on the road west from Paris, with a leper house. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Honoré; the church of Saint-Philippe-du-Roule keeps its name.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la route partant de Paris vers l'ouest, avec une léproserie. Il fut absorbé par le faubourg Saint-Honoré ; l'église Saint-Philippe-du-Roule en garde le nom.
places.summary_sv: En by vid vägen västerut från Paris, med ett leprasjukhus. Den uppgick i faubourg Saint-Honoré; kyrkan Saint-Philippe-du-Roule bär fortfarande dess namn.
places.detail: First mentioned in thirteenth-century charters, the hamlet was originally a dependency of Villiers-la-Garenne. Around 1200, the moneyers of the Paris mint purchased a property here to care for members suffering from leprosy, and Bishop Pierre de Nemours authorized a chapel in 1217. As leprosy waned by the mid-sixteenth century, the guild leased the estate to its officers as a country retreat under the patronage of Saints Philip and James. The village, depicted on the map with a few houses and windmills, comprised two hamlets, the Bas-Roule and Haut-Roule. In 1639, Louis XIII permitted residents to build and unite with the neighbouring village of La Ville-l'Évêque. The parish church was rebuilt between 1768 and 1784 to designs by the architect Chalgrin.

places.summary: A village on the hill west of Paris above the Seine. It was annexed in 1860; the Palais de Chaillot stands at the top of the hill.
places.summary_fr: Un village sur la colline à l'ouest de Paris, au-dessus de la Seine. Il fut annexé en 1860 ; le palais de Chaillot se dresse au sommet de la colline.
places.summary_sv: En by på kullen väster om Paris ovanför Seine. Den införlivades 1860; Palais de Chaillot står på kullens topp.
places.detail: In 1060, Henri I gave the church of Chaillot to the canons of Sainte-Geneviève, and Chaillot became the main parish of the priory of Saint-Martin. During the Middle Ages, a village surrounded by vineyards developed along a single road and became known for its wine. In 1360, during the Hundred Years' War, nuns fleeing the pillaged abbey of Longchamp bought a house here, creating a sub-fief that split the parish in two. On 6 March 1472, King Louis XI seized high justice over Chaillot, granting the territory two years later to his grand chamberlain Philippe de Commynes. In 1493, Anne of Brittany donated the nearby manor of Nigeon to the Minim order.

places.summary: A village west of Paris on the Seine, later a favourite country retreat of writers such as Molière and Boileau. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 16th arrondissement.
places.summary_fr: Un village à l'ouest de Paris, au bord de la Seine, plus tard lieu de villégiature apprécié d'écrivains comme Molière et Boileau. Il fut annexé à Paris en 1860 et fait aujourd'hui partie du XVIe arrondissement.
places.summary_sv: En by väster om Paris vid Seine, senare ett omtyckt sommarnöje för författare som Molière och Boileau. Den införlivades med Paris 1860 och är i dag en del av 16:e arrondissementet.

places.note: Hue-Leu, the old name of the rue du Grand-Hurleur: 'very well named here' (Cousin 1875)
places.summary: Hue-Leu, the medieval name of the rue du Grand-Hurleur; Cousin (1875) notes that it is 'very well named here'. It disappeared when the boulevard de Sébastopol was cut through.
places.summary_fr: Hue-Leu, le nom médiéval de la rue du Grand-Hurleur ; Cousin (1875) note qu'elle est « très bien nommée ici ». Elle disparut lors du percement du boulevard de Sébastopol.
places.summary_sv: Hue-Leu, det medeltida namnet på rue du Grand-Hurleur; Cousin (1875) noterar att den är ”mycket väl namngiven här”. Den försvann när boulevard de Sébastopol drogs fram.
places.detail: The street ran from the rue Saint-Martin to the now vanished rue du Bourg l'Abbé. Documented in 1253 under the variants Heuleu, Huleu, and Hue Leu, it was also known at times as the rue du Pet and the rue des Innocents.

places.note: the rue Tiron or Tison, printed 'R. de Ison' (Cousin 1875)
places.summary: The rue Tiron or Tison, printed 'R. de Ison', recorded in 1250 (Jules Cousin, 1875).
places.summary_fr: La rue Tiron ou Tison, imprimée « R. de Ison », mentionnée en 1250 (Jules Cousin, 1875).
places.summary_sv: Rue Tiron eller Tison, tryckt ”R. de Ison”, omnämnd 1250 (Jules Cousin, 1875).

places.old: LA VILLE CITE VNIVERSITE DE PARIS
places.note: the title banderole across the top of the sheet
places.summary: The map's own title, on a banderole across the top: the town, the city and the university of Paris. Those were the three parts of the city at the time — the Ville on the right bank, the Cité on the island, the Université on the left bank.
places.summary_fr: Le titre du plan, sur une banderole en haut : la ville, la cité et l’université de Paris. C’étaient les trois parties de la ville à l’époque : la Ville sur la rive droite, la Cité dans l’île, l’Université sur la rive gauche.
places.summary_sv: Kartans egen titel, på ett banderoll överst: staden, Cité och universitetet i Paris. Det var stadens tre delar på den tiden — Ville på högra stranden, Cité på ön och Université på vänstra stranden.

places.note: crowned shield, three fleurs-de-lis, ringed by a collar of scallop shells; no printed text
places.summary: The arms of the kingdom: three golden fleurs-de-lis on blue, under a crown and ringed by a collar of scallop shells. They stand at the top of the sheet, facing the arms of Paris.
places.summary_fr: Les armes du royaume : trois fleurs de lis d’or sur azur, sous une couronne et entourées d’un collier de coquilles. Elles occupent le haut du plan, face aux armes de Paris.
places.summary_sv: Rikets vapen: tre gyllene liljor på blått, under en krona och omgivna av en krage av musselskal. De står överst på arket, mitt emot Paris vapen.

places.note: a ship under a chief of fleurs-de-lis; no printed text
places.summary: The arms of Paris: a ship on red, under a chief of golden fleurs-de-lis. They face the arms of France across the top of the sheet.
places.summary_fr: Les armes de Paris : une nef sur gueules, sous un chef de fleurs de lis d’or. Elles font face aux armes de France en haut du plan.
places.summary_sv: Paris vapen: ett skepp på rött, under ett huvud av gyllene liljor. De står mitt emot Frankrikes vapen överst på arket.

places.note: King Henri II's emblem, between the arms of France and Subsolanus; no printed text
places.summary: Three interlaced crescents, the emblem of King Henri II (reigned 1547–1559), between the arms of France and the east wind.
places.summary_fr: Trois croissants entrelacés, l’emblème du roi Henri II (1547–1559), entre les armes de France et le vent d’est.
places.summary_sv: Tre sammanflätade halvmånar, kung Henrik II:s emblem (regent 1547–1559), mellan Frankrikes vapen och östanvinden.

places.old: A POEM IN PRAISE OF PARIS
places.note: 108 lines in two panels; the second panel is also_px
places.summary: A poem of 108 lines in praise of Paris, printed in two panels at the foot of the sheet. The initials of its first fourteen lines spell GILLES CORROSET — the poet and bookseller Gilles Corrozet. Transcribed and translated line by line on the texts page.
places.summary_fr: Un poème de 108 vers à la louange de Paris, imprimé en deux cartouches au bas du plan. Les initiales des quatorze premiers vers forment GILLES CORROSET — le poète et libraire Gilles Corrozet. Transcrit et traduit vers par vers sur la page des textes.
places.summary_sv: En dikt på 108 rader till Paris lov, tryckt i två fält nedtill på arket. Begynnelsebokstäverna i de första fjorton raderna bildar GILLES CORROSET — poeten och bokhandlaren Gilles Corrozet. Transkriberad och översatt rad för rad på textsidan.

places.note: Icy est le vray pourtraict naturel de la ville, cite, vniuersite...
places.summary: The publishers' notice, and the counts the map claims for itself: 287 streets and alleys, 104 churches and monasteries, 49 colleges. It ends with the address — Olivier Truschet and Germain Hoyau, in the rue de Montorgueil, at the Chef Saint-Denis.
places.summary_fr: L’avis des éditeurs, et les nombres que le plan revendique : 287 rues et ruelles, 104 églises et monastères, 49 collèges. Il se termine par l’adresse : Olivier Truschet et Germain Hoyau, rue de Montorgueil, au Chef Saint-Denis.
places.summary_sv: Utgivarnas meddelande, och de tal kartan själv anger: 287 gator och gränder, 104 kyrkor och kloster, 49 kollegier. Det slutar med adressen — Olivier Truschet och Germain Hoyau, vid rue de Montorgueil, au Chef Saint-Denis.

places.note: the Basel library's oval stamp, bottom-left corner
places.summary: The oval stamp of the public library of Basel, in the bottom-left corner. Basel's copy is the only one known; the librarian Louis Sieber recognised it in 1874.
places.summary_fr: Le cachet ovale de la bibliothèque publique de Bâle, dans le coin inférieur gauche. L’exemplaire de Bâle est le seul connu ; le bibliothécaire Louis Sieber l’a identifié en 1874.
places.summary_sv: Den ovala stämpeln från det offentliga biblioteket i Basel, i nedre vänstra hörnet. Basels exemplar är det enda kända; bibliotekarien Louis Sieber identifierade det 1874.
